extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (authors, referees, editors), especially combinatorics researchers and journal editors
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critique on mathematical journals, peer review practices (single/double blind, paid refereeing, simultaneous submissions), editorial policies, and strategies for authors and referees — with a focus on how these affect combinatorics. Includes concrete proposed procedural reforms (quick opinions, staged review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal anti-combinatorics bias / publication record
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal may exhibit an implicit or explicit bias against Combinatorics if its publication record shows few or no combinatorics papers (examples cited: AJM, CJM, Compositio, Publ. Math. IHÉS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check MathSciNet / MSC primary classifications (e.g., 05) and paper counts; ask editors directly whether a bias exists; use evidence (zero or near-zero publications) to judge whether a journal is receptive to your area. Possible actions: submit best work anyway (especially if tenured), ask referees/editors about policy, or publicly 'shame' journals if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board composition / area representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal has editors in a given area (e.g., combinatorics) affects likelihood of acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect editorial board for specialists in your field. Lack of in-area editors can lead to quick opinions or external referees unfamiliar with the topic, increasing rejection risk. Presence of trusted editors (even a single associate editor) can improve chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between stated scope and actual publications
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal's stated scope (e.g., 'spanning the range of mathematics') should be compared to the distribution of areas it actually publishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If most papers come from a few 'grandfathered' areas, the journal's claim to span mathematics is suspect. Use breakdowns (e.g., ZbMATH) to evaluate whether the journal's practice aligns with its mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active solicitation and encouragement of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals that want work in an area will make an effort to attract it (soliciting submissions, encouraging top people to submit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer journals that proactively invite submissions or explicitly encourage your field; such journals are more likely to consider high-quality combinatorics work despite low overall area share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask editors when requested to referee: 'Does your journal have a bias against X?'
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to provide quick opinions or referee reports, explicitly ask editors whether the journal has bias against the relevant area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the editor denies bias but then rejects positive reports, follow up. This is a way to test editorial openness and to hold editors accountable; aim to 'exhaust' them with follow-up questions about acceptance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic submission behavior (don't boycott; submit best work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not boycott journals perceived as biased; instead, consider submitting best work (especially if tenured) to maintain pressure and visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boycotts are counterproductive because journals are already excluding the work. Submitting top papers can force journals to address perceived bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of peer review / value of neutral vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review provides a neutral vetting process that identifies errors, improves papers through iterative revision, and discourages shortcuts in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abolishing peer review risks lowering standards, encouraging unsalvageable incorrect work, and advantaging well-connected authors. For math, careful refereeing and rounds of revision are crucial for correctness and community trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of abolishing peer review (systemic consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing peer review could lead to journals favoring the well-known, junior researchers losing publication routes, increased incorrect results, harmful hiring/grant changes, and eventual decline of deep areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these systemic downstream effects when evaluating proposals to remove peer review; weigh short-term openness against long-term structural harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous submissions to multiple journals — practical and legal risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing simultaneous submissions would overwhelm referees, foster editorial refusal, spawn chatrooms about who referees what, and prompt publishers to demand signed conditional copyright transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of proposals for simultaneous submissions: they create reviewer overload and legal/career risks, and could result in journals implementing punitive copyright policies (or universities enforcing them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-anonymizing referees (open review) — tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Making referees' identities public gives credit but may reduce willingness to referee due to COI and risks to collegial relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening referee identities can be good for credit, but in small subfields anonymity preserves ambiguity that protects referees from social fallout; expect fewer willing referees if reports are signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying referees — unintended consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying referees seems attractive to improve participation, but high per-paper costs would divert journals toward APC-funded models and create perverse incentives (acceptance bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate realistic referee pay (e.g., $100/hr × 10–20 hours = $1–2K per report). Only wealthy open-access models could absorb this, raising pay-to-publish corruption concerns and selection biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-anonymous (double blind) refereeing — stated goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind refereeing aims 'to reduce the effect of initial impressions and biases' (so referees judge impact, interest, and writing rather than author identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind can reduce institutional/reputation bias and has evidence of benefits in some fields. It is more workable in rapid-conference settings; journals must weigh benefits against practical issues arising from long review timelines and arXiv availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind drawbacks: harms to juniors, benefits to serial submitters, and risks from cranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity can disadvantage juniors (who may need reputation to overcome low status), help serial submitters/self-plagiarists and cranks/fraudsters by masking past behavior, and reduce referees' willingness to invest time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing double-blind, consider safeguards: if referees can't identify authors, they may spend more time per paper, or conversely may be less willing to mentor/improve submissions. Editors should monitor these effects and possibly require staged disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reality of double-blind in long journal processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Long review times make it likely referees will find or 'google' authors anyway (e.g., prior related papers), reducing the theoretical benefits of double-blind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should acknowledge enforceability limits; consider staged processes where anonymity is used only in an initial quick stage but authors' names provided for full review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for gradual, small-scale experimentation (pilot changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt modest, incremental reforms (pilots in low-stakes venues) rather than sweeping overhaul: TCS conferences tested double-blind and rebuttal stages first, then scaled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot changes in smaller venues to work out kinks (COI, enforcement) before imposing them on top journals. Learn from conference experience (rebuttals, staged decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal stage usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: A rebuttal stage (authors respond to reviewer comments) can reduce superficial nitpicking and clarify substantive issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rapid-review contexts this is helpful; journals should consider adding a rebuttal stage to allow authors to correct misunderstandings and prevent random negative decisions based on shallow first impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Quick opinion' staged review proposal (stage i)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a quick-opinion window (3–4 weeks): referees asked for a quick opinion can agree/decline within 48 hours and provide a short (1–2 paragraph) assessment of fit based on the introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect 2–3 quick opinions to screen for suitability. If an editor requests more, that may indicate bias or fishing for negative opinion. This stage models practices at Nature/Science and TCS conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quick opinions anonymous and return them to authors (stage ii and iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick-opinion requests should be anonymous; reviewers assess fit and these brief opinions should be returned to authors. If a paper is rejected after this stage, quick opinions may be sent to another journal upon resubmission without revealing reviewer names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects reviewers while giving authors useful early feedback; it also facilitates transfer of succinct assessments across journals without exposing reviewers' identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect reviewer anonymity across resubmissions (stage iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: If quick opinions are forwarded to another editor, do not disclose reviewer identities to protect them from becoming semi-public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should pass only opinions, not reviewer names. If a receiving editor distrusts the prior editor, they can collect new quick opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective journals: require papers be unavailable online during quick-opinion stage (stage iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top selective journals could require that the paper not be publicly available during the quick-opinion window; violations risk rejection without review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A submission timestamp serves as a priority certificate. A short embargo (3 weeks) is unlikely to harm authors, and prevents easy de-anonymization during initial screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-stage full review with author names revealed (stage v)
rubrics_metrics.description: After quick-opinion screening, move to full review with referees receiving authors' names and proceed per usual practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This staged approach retains some early anonymity benefits while enabling informed, thorough review when it matters most, leveraging knowledge of authors' past work in the detailed referee stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees should judge by authors' past work and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of an author's previous work and reputation helps referees assess whether to spend significant time improving a submission (especially to help junior or under-resourced authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors are anonymous, referees may be less inclined to mentor or invest large effort; editors should consider this tradeoff when choosing review formats. For borderline/early-career authors, knowledge can prompt constructive, detailed reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees should compare with updated versions during long review delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Because journal review can take many months or years, referees should check for updated versions and account for public scrutiny that may have improved the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long timelines justify referees looking at newer versions or arXiv updates before finalizing judgments; this maintains fairness and leverages public corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sweeping, rapid reforms; prefer small incremental changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale abrupt changes to peer review are risky; modest, careful modifications implemented slowly are recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the TCS model: experiment in lower-stakes venues, iterate, and scale what works while monitoring for unintended side-effects (COI, reviewer availability, quality changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all mathematics should be published
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication decisions require judgment: 'Not all math deserves to be published, just like not all math needs to be done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and referees should apply selection criteria (significance, correctness, novelty, clarity) rather than accepting everything. Authors should aim for substantive contributions rather than quantity.
